subject: Art & Design
title: Understanding White Balance: Why Colors Shift
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Understanding White Balance: Why Colors Shift.

hook.text: Indoor photos look orange. Shade photos look blue. Your eyes auto-correct. Your camera doesn't.

buildup.text: White balance adjusts how the camera interprets color temperature — measured in Kelvin.

discovery.text: Daylight is ~5500K (neutral). Tungsten bulbs are ~3200K (warm). Shade is ~7000K (cool blue).

twist.text: Auto white balance works 80% of the time. The other 20% — mixed lighting, creative intent — requires manual control.

climax.text: Shooting RAW lets you change white balance later without quality loss. It's the safety net of color.

punchline.text: The 'wrong' white balance can be the right creative choice.

quiz.question: Why do indoor photos often look orange?
options: Tungsten bulbs emit warm light around 3200K that the camera captures
Cameras add orange filters indoors automatically
Indoor air particles scatter orange light

details.summary: White balance corrects color casts caused by different light sources — tungsten bulbs create warm orange tones, shade creates cool blue tones, and fluorescent lighting creates green. Setting the correct white balance ensures whites appear neutral, though intentional color casts can enhance mood.
details.whyItMatters: Incorrect white balance makes images look unnatural — orange skin under tungsten, blue cast in shade. Understanding white balance gives photographers control over color accuracy and the ability to use color temperature creatively.
takeaways: Different light sources create different color temperatures
White balance corrects unwanted color casts
Intentional color casts can enhance mood creatively

faq.question: Should you shoot in auto white balance?
faq.answer: Auto white balance works well for most situations and is a safe default. However, it can shift between frames in inconsistent lighting, creating color mismatches in a series.

faq.question: Can white balance be fixed in editing?
faq.answer: Yes, if shooting in RAW format. RAW files preserve all color data, allowing complete white balance adjustment in post-processing with no quality loss. JPEG files compress color data, making correction possible but with some quality degradation. This is a major reason to shoot RAW.
